source_review.notes: Reviewed all ten references. CSP event/process foundations were checked against Hoare's paper/book; channel types, close, receive, and select semantics against the current Go specification and official guidance; ownership/topology against Rust std and the Rust Book; async MPSC lifecycle/cancellation against Tokio documentation; coroutine channels against Kotlin docs; and alternative/parking semantics against core.async docs. Concrete language behavior is not generalized beyond its API.

evidence: Definitions and Notation defines capacity K, queue Q, send/receive indicators, process wait graph G=(P,E), and rendezvous event c.v.
Rendezvous, enqueue, dequeue, processing, effect, close, and disconnect remain distinct events throughout.
notation_and_syntax.notes: Capacity, accounting, graph, transition, and trace terminology was checked for consistent scope.

evidence: artifacts/snippets/CONPAR-039/report.json records two initial accepts, one would-block, one later accept, three receives, max depth two, and zero remaining.
Independent replay yields received 10,20,30, sum 60, accepted three, capacity never above two, and closed only after drain.
numerical_recomputation.notes: Send outcomes, values, occupancy, sum, close state, stdout, and empty stderr match exact evidence.

evidence: Every buffered transition preserves 0<=|Q|<=K; direct handoff is explicitly separated from queue increments/decrements.
Under reliable transfer and complete drain, sum S_i=sum R_i; discard/failure/cancellation require additional terminal categories rather than hidden loss.
symbolic_recomputation.notes: The wait-graph cycle is labeled a deadlock candidate until ready alternatives, close, timeout, and external progress are excluded.

evidence: Reviewed capacity zero/one/full/unbounded, direct handoff, multiple senders/receivers, multiple-ready select, default spin, unfairness, send/receive cancellation, and close with buffered values.
Reviewed retained clones, receiver exit, work/result cycles, locks/permits, worker crash after receive, upstream early stop, distributed delivery, shutdown, and safety-critical handoff.
boundary_and_adversarial_cases.notes: Boundary review spans synchronization, ownership, capacity, fairness, cancellation, failure, topology, lifecycle, and deployment risks.

evidence: Successful sends have one declared ownership outcome; channel occupancy stays bounded; endpoint clones and one close authority are accounted for.
Selection withdraws losers under API rules, blocking operations hold no peer-needed resource, and shutdown closes/drains/discards and joins every process.
invariant_checking.notes: Invariants were checked across send, receive, block, wake, select, cancel, close, drain, disconnect, failure, and join.

evidence: The bounded-queue induction starts at zero and each accepted send/receive transition preserves the capacity interval.
The coordinator/workers wait-cycle proof identifies mutual wait edges and explains why larger finite buffers postpone but do not remove the topology cycle.
proof_review.notes: Arguments apply to the stated model/API and do not prove scheduler fairness, network delivery, or application exactly-once effects.

evidence: CSP, Go, Rust std, Tokio, Kotlin, and core.async claims are attributed to their model/API.
Executable limitations exclude threads, atomics, visibility, wakeups, rendezvous, select, fairness, cancellation, failures, clones, networks, and cleanup.
proof_sketch_labeling.notes: Formal CSP concepts, concrete runtime contracts, deterministic queue evidence, and external review remain distinct.

evidence: python3 tools/verify_snippets.py CONPAR-039 passed the exact capacity/close trace with recorded Python version, stdout, and stderr.
Wait latency, fairness, scheduler behavior, memory visibility, network delivery, and physical response are explicitly empirical/runtime-specific.
empirical_evidence_labeling.notes: The run validates one nonblocking teaching queue only and proves no real channel or CSP implementation behavior.

conceptual_review.notes: Reviewed CSP events, rendezvous/buffering, ownership/visibility, topology, close/drain, select/fairness, wait graphs, cancellation, typed protocols, fan-in/out, pipelines, distributed channels, shutdown, observability, and deterministic tests.

practitioner_review.notes: Reviewed count/byte bounds, endpoint-clone ledgers, typed close causes, select tie/default policy, lock-free blocking boundaries, cancellation commitment, stable result identity, upstream early-stop propagation, dependency-ordered closure, and exact terminal accounting.

pedagogical_review.notes: The review sheet states channel/CSP distinctions; exposition progresses from events to lifecycle; the executable trace demonstrates full/would-block/drain; ten examples are nonduplicative; and five exercises progress from capacity to railway-safety transfer with complete answers.

limitations: Internal authoring and verification evidence only; no external channel-runtime, formal-methods, distributed-systems, security, nuclear, railway, regulatory, real-time, or functional-safety review is claimed. The teaching model does not establish synchronization, visibility, fairness, cancellation, failure, network, shutdown, or deployment correctness.
